title: Would the tests have caught the known cases?
question: For each organization in a proven, charged or officially reported case, did any of this project’s warning signs show in the records before the matter became public, and how long before?
finding: 216 case files at those three levels name 72 organizations that can be matched to a City payee; 150 further names (firms the City never paid under that name, unnamed parties and groups) cannot be tested at all. For 39 of the 72, at least one sign is dated to a fiscal year before the matter became public, the earliest by a middle figure of 6 years; 33 show nothing firmly dated before it, 12 of them carrying no sign at all today. Counting only the 21 kinds of sign that the next screen finds informative, 32 had at least one dated before, the earliest by a middle figure of 5 years. But a sign before the date is common everywhere: 65% of the 355 other profiled nonprofits carry one dated before fiscal 2025, against 79% of the 42 known-case nonprofits. What differs is how many: a middle figure of 4 such signs for the known cases against 1 for the rest. The informative signs most often dated before: A gift, donation or requested payment in the year one of its contracts was approved (20); Identical odd amounts paid twice in one year (15); Three or more kinds of dated dealing with one official inside two years (this file) (12); Agreements that at least doubled through amendments (7).
how: Known cases are the case files marked proven, charged or official. The date a matter became public is the earliest timeline entry of the kind “enforcement” that names the organization, or failing that the earliest such entry in its most serious case file (where a file has no enforcement entry, its earliest entry citing an official report). Each warning sign the organization carries today was dated: recomputed year by year from dated records where the rule is simple (awards without bidding, contracts just under $10 million, approvals after the fact, purchase orders under the limit, duplicate payments, monitoring findings, registration dates, gifts, donations in the approval window, and the chains in this file); otherwise from the fiscal years its own sentence cites (one year later where the sentence rests on a tax return or an audit, which this test treats as public the year after; a running total “since” a year is treated as running to fiscal 2026). A sign counts as “before” only if the last year it cites is earlier than the fiscal year the matter became public; if its years span that date it is “possibly before”. The comparison group is every profiled nonprofit in no case file, measured as if its matter had become public in the fiscal year of the middle known case.
limits: An organization named in a case file is not always the one accused: several are funders, fiscal sponsors or counterparties. To keep the test from being circular, 16 kinds of sign are left out because they record an enforcement step or exist only because the organization was already flagged (listed in this file under leftOut), and the case flag itself is never counted. Signs dated from their own sentence are approximate to a year, and 73 sign-instances carry no year and are not counted either way. Payment records begin in fiscal 2017 and award-method records in fiscal 2019, so a case that became public before about fiscal 2020 could not have been caught by tests that need them. Well-known organizations have been looked at harder by every screen, which flatters the result. With 72 organizations, none of these counts supports a rate. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
